content: Eravacycline is indicated for the treatment of complicated intra-abdominal infections (cIAIs) at a dosage of 1 mg/kg administered intravenously every 12 hours for a duration of 4 to 14 days. The intravenous infusion should be given over approximately 60 minutes. No dosage adjustment is required for patients with renal impairment. However, it is not indicated for the treatment of complicated urinary tract infections. The safety and efficacy of eravacycline in patients under 18 years of age have not been established. Eravacycline may reduce the effectiveness of amoxicillin and ampicillin due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Tetracyclines, including eravacycline, can interfere with the bactericidal action of penicillins. If used concomitantly, monitor for reduced therapeutic effects of penicillins. It is recommended to avoid or use alternative drugs in such cases. Eravacycline can decrease the efficacy of oral microbiota products, which contain bacterial spores, due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Antibacterial agents may reduce the effectiveness of these products if co-administered. It is advised to complete antibiotic regimens 2 to 4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. Systemic retinoid use, such as palovarotene, has been associated with benign intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri), particularly when used with tetracyclines. Avoid or use alternative drugs in such cases. Magnesium sulfate or potassium chloride can reduce eravacycline levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. To avoid chelation with magnesium, administer tetracyclines at least 2 hours before and no less than 6 hours after each dose. Eravacycline may increase the effects of warfarin through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. Zinc can decrease the levels or effects of eravacycline by cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. Modify therapy and monitor closely. Separate the administration of oral tetracycline derivatives and oral zinc salts by at least 2 hours. Adverse effects associated with eravacycline include palpitations, acute pancreatitis, pancreatic necrosis, chest pain, hypersensitivity reactions, and laboratory abnormalities such as increased amylase, lipase, ALT, and GGT levels, prolonged aPTT, decreased creatinine clearance, reduced white blood cell count, and neutropenia. Other reported effects include hypocalcemia, dizziness, dysgeusia, anxiety, insomnia, depression, pleural effusion, dyspnea, rash, and excessive sweating. Hypersensitivity to eravacycline, tetracycline antibacterials, or any excipients is a contraindication. Life-threatening hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported. Discontinue use if an allergic reaction occurs. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, ranging from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinue any ongoing antibacterial drugs not directed against C. difficile and initiate appropriate treatment. Eravacycline is structurally similar to tetracyclines and may cause similar adverse reactions, including photosensitivity, pseudotumor cerebri, and anti-anabolic effects, which can lead to increased BUN, azotemia, acidosis, hyperphosphatemia, pancreatitis, and abnormal liver function tests. It may also cause overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms, including fungi. Prescribing eravacycline without a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of drug-resistant bacteria. Like other tetracycline-class antibacterial drugs, eravacycline may cause discoloration of deciduous teeth and reversible inhibition of bone growth when administered during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy. It is unknown if eravacycline is excreted in human breast milk, but it is excreted in the milk of lactating rats. Since other antibacterial options are available for treating cIAI in lactating women and due to the potential for serious adverse reactions, including tooth discoloration and inhibition of bone growth, breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment and for 4 days after the last dose. Controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk, making eravacycline generally acceptable for use during pregnancy. However, caution is advised, and alternative treatments should be considered when possible.
